D1:
Why: Core is the LOWEST AnimationPriority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). The default Animate script plays idle/walk at Idle/Movement, which outrank Core, so they win the blend on the arm joints and your swing barely shows. Also Humanoid:LoadAnimation is deprecated, and loading a new track on every click leaks tracks.
Fix: re-export the clip as Action (or Action2+), or override at runtime; load once via the Animator.
```lua
local char = player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()
local animator = char:WaitForChild("Humanoid"):WaitForChild("Animator")
local swing = animator:LoadAnimation(script.SwingAnim) -- load once, cache
swing.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    swing:Play()
end)
```
Reload the track on CharacterAdded (new Animator). Don't sort by Priority.Value, because Core's enum value is 1000 even though it is the lowest.
D2:
1) Server Script: the camera is client-side. workspace.CurrentCamera on the server is not the player's camera, so writing to it does nothing. Camera code must run in a LocalScript (the server can trigger it with a RemoteEvent).
2) Snap back: with CameraType = Custom, the default PlayerModule camera script overwrites Camera.CFrame every frame and puts it back behind the character.
Fix:
```lua
local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Scriptable
cam.CFrame = workspace.CutsceneCam.CFrame -- or tween it
-- when the cutscene ends:
cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Custom
cam.CameraSubject = player.Character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
```
Always restore Custom, including on death/CharacterRemoving/errors (add a watchdog), or the player gets stuck in the cutscene camera.
D3:
CanvasSize is fixed at 600 px. The UIListLayout places all the cloned buttons, but the scrollable canvas stays 600 px tall, so items past 600 px can't be reached (and with 8 items there is empty scroll space). Using scale in CanvasSize doesn't help either: scale is relative to the frame, not the content.
Cleanest fix: set ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y and CanvasSize = UDim2.new(0, 0, 0, 0). The canvas then grows to fit the layout content. Set ScrollingDirection = Y and VerticalScrollBarInset = ScrollBar (or add padding) so the bar doesn't cover items.
Manual alternative: listen to UIListLayout:GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteContentSize") and set CanvasSize = UDim2.fromOffset(0, layout.AbsoluteContentSize.Y + padding). For very long lists (hundreds of items), compute the size and virtualize the list.
D4:
Problems:
1) Too little force: 5000 is below the weight. Lift needs Force >= AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity (gravity defaults to 196.2). A 20x2x20 plastic part (~800 stud^3 at density 0.7) weighs about 560 mass * 196.2 = ~110,000.
2) Off-center application: the force acts at the corner Attachment0, so it also creates a torque and the platform tips.
3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force rotates with the part. Once it tilts, the "up" force gains a sideways part and pushes it to slide and spin.
Correct setup: put the attachment at the center (or set ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true), and set RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World with Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity * k, 0) (k slightly above 1 to rise, 1 to hover). A constant VectorForce has no speed cap and no height control, so add damping or a controller, or use AlignPosition/LinearVelocity for height. Add AlignOrientation (OneAttachment, PrimaryAxisParallel to world up) to keep it level. Give the server network ownership, or anchor while idle.
D5:
Leaks:
1) sessions[player] is never cleared, so every Player object plus its kills/history stays in memory forever (the history table grows too).
2) Each CharacterAdded makes a new Heartbeat connection that is never disconnected. Each respawn adds another one that keeps running updateAura on dead characters and keeps them referenced. Heartbeat is long-lived, so destroying the character doesn't disconnect it.
3) Unbounded history growth: cap it (ring buffer).
Fix:
```lua
local sessions = {}
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local s = { kills = 0, history = {}, conns = {} }
    sessions[player] = s
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(char)
        if s.aura then s.aura:Disconnect() end
        s.aura = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function() updateAura(char) end)
        char.Destroying:Once(function()
            if s.aura then s.aura:Disconnect(); s.aura = nil end
        end)
    end)
end)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    local s = sessions[player]
    if s and s.aura then s.aura:Disconnect() end
    sessions[player] = nil
end)
```
Better: one Heartbeat loop over all live characters instead of one per player. Check the fix by measuring the memory slope after warm-up (Dev Console).

```lua
local PathfindingService = game:GetService("PathfindingService")
local path = PathfindingService:CreatePath({
    AgentRadius = 2, AgentHeight = 5, AgentCanJump = true,
    Costs = { Lava = math.huge, Water = 20 },
})
local function moveTo(humanoid: Humanoid, target: Vector3)
    local root = humanoid.RootPart
    local ok = pcall(path.ComputeAsync, path, root.Position, target)
    if not ok or path.Status ~= Enum.PathStatus.Success then return false end
    for _, wp in path:GetWaypoints() do
        if wp.Action == Enum.PathWaypointAction.Jump then
            humanoid.Jump = true
        end
        humanoid:MoveTo(wp.Position)
        local reached = humanoid.MoveToFinished:Wait() -- add a timeout in production
        if not reached then return false end
    end
    return true
end
```
Rules:
- Costs keys are PathfindingModifier Labels or Enum.Material names. math.huge = never traversed, so Lava is fully blocked. A finite cost (Water = 20) means "avoid if a reasonable route exists".
- PathfindingModifier parts: anchored, CanCollide off, Label = "Lava" (PassThrough only for doors).
- AgentCanJump = true and handle PathWaypointAction.Jump by jumping before the waypoint.
- ComputeAsync yields and can fail (distance/node limits), so pcall it and check Status.
- Use path.Blocked to recompute. Use per-waypoint MoveToFinished timeouts (MoveTo gives up after 8 s). Server-own the NPC root (SetNetworkOwner(nil)). Throttle path requests.

D11:
Cars: give the driver network ownership while seated (VehicleSeat does this automatically, or call SetNetworkOwner(player) on the chassis when Occupant changes). The driver then simulates locally with no input latency, which fixes the lag. When they exit, go back to SetNetworkOwnershipAuto, or server-own/anchor parked and empty cars. With several seats, use one VehicleSeat for the driver and plain Seats for passengers.
NPC guards: call SetNetworkOwner(nil) on every guard's assembly root after spawn so the server always simulates them. With automatic ownership, a guard near a player gets handed to that client, and that client can then fling, teleport or control it.
Security: whoever owns a part can set its position and velocity freely (teleport, fly, fling with huge/NaN velocity, fake Touched). So a driver can teleport their own car. Ownership gives authority over physics, not trust. Mitigate on the server: check car speed and position deltas against max speed (reset or eject on violation), clamp velocities, never award anything based on client-owned Touched, do distance checks at event time, and keep hitboxes and damage server-side. Keep guards server-owned and anchor or server-own important props. (2026: Server Authority mode is the engine-level option for competitive games.)
D12:
What the engine keeps: standard DataStores have automatic versioning. A version (backup) is kept for the first write per key per UTC hour, and superseded versions are kept for 30 days. RemoveAsync is also recoverable through versions. OrderedDataStores have no version history.
Tool (server/Studio admin or Open Cloud):
```lua
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local key = "Player_" .. userId
local cutoffMs = updateTimeUnix * 1000
local ok, value, info = pcall(store.GetVersionAtTimeAsync, store, key, cutoffMs)
-- or ListVersionsAsync(key, Enum.SortDirection.Descending, 0, cutoffMs, 10) + GetVersionAsync(key, versionId)
if ok and value then
    store:SetAsync(key, value, info and info:GetUserIds(), info and info:GetMetadata())
end
```
GetVersionAtTimeAsync returns the version that was current at that timestamp. Writing it back creates a new version, so the restore itself can be undone.
Limits: only hourly granularity (several writes in one hour keep only the first), so the "just before" state may be up to an hour old. 30-day window. Restore only while the player is offline, or lock their session first, or their live server autosave overwrites it. Calls use the same experience read/write budgets. Values max ~4 MB. Log every restore. Creator Hub's Data Stores Manager can also revert a key by hand. Session-lock and migration code must accept the restored schema.
D13:
Architecture: web panel -> your backend (holds Open Cloud API keys in a secret manager, with auth and audit log) -> Roblox Open Cloud.
(1) Announcements: backend calls the Open Cloud MessagingService publish endpoint (universe messaging, e.g. topic "Announce"). Each server subscribes with MessagingService:SubscribeAsync("Announce") and shows the text to its players through a RemoteEvent. Limits: 1 KB message, best-effort delivery (~1-2 s, no ordering or guarantee). Include an id so servers ignore duplicates. Optionally also write the announcement to a DataStore/MemoryStore so servers that start late can read it.
(2) Grants: don't edit live profiles directly. Write a pending grant to a "PendingGrants" key/queue for the userId through Open Cloud DataStore (v2 entries API) or a MemoryStore queue, with a unique grantId. Then publish a "grant" message. The server that has the player online (or the next server they join, on load) claims the grant atomically with UpdateAsync, applies it to the profile, and marks the grantId as consumed (idempotent, so no double grants). Editing an offline player's main key directly from Open Cloud is risky because there is no UpdateAsync transform and it can race a live session.
Security: one API key per purpose with minimal scopes (messaging publish; datastore read/update on specific stores), restricted to the experience, with expiry and rotation. Honor 429/retry-after with backoff. Open Cloud writes share the experience's DataStore budget. Validate item ids server-side.
D14:
BindableEvent/BindableFunction arguments are serialized and copied the same way remotes are: each handler gets its own deep copy of the table. Metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table without its class methods (inv:Add() is nil -> error). Functions are dropped, non-string keys become strings, mixed or sparse arrays can lose entries, and changes the receiver makes to its copy never reach the sender's object, so state drifts apart. (Instance references like the Player do survive.)
ModuleScripts fix this: require() runs a module once per Luau environment and returns the same cached table to every server script. A shared InventoryService module (e.g. InventoryService.get(player) returning the live OOP object) lets all systems call methods on the same object directly, with no copying, and with types/autocomplete. Use direct function calls or a pure-Luau Signal module for in-process events (those pass references and keep metatables), and keep BindableEvents for loose, primitive-only messages. Structure: a few Scripts that bootstrap service modules, with services requiring each other. Note that server and client get separate module copies, so cross-boundary communication still needs remotes.
D15:
UnreliableRemoteEvent suits high-frequency, cosmetic, replaceable data where only the latest value matters: aim direction, look angles, footstep/VFX cues, positions of cheap objects. Dropping one is harmless because the next update replaces it. It doesn't wait for retransmits or ordering, so it doesn't block the reliable queue, and reliable events (hits, purchases) stop waiting behind the 30 Hz spam.
Constraints:
- Delivery is not guaranteed and order is not guaranteed. Add sequence numbers (with wraparound) and drop stale ones. Interpolate on the receiver.
- Payload limit is about 1,000 bytes (older docs said 900; design for under 900). Larger payloads are dropped, not split. Send compact data (e.g. a buffer or quantized angles).
- Throttled excess is dropped, not delayed.
- Never use it for state changes, ability start/stop, hits, damage or purchases. Those stay on RemoteEvent with server validation.
- The server still validates: check types, finite numbers (math.isfinite), unit-length vectors, and a per-player rate limit before re-broadcasting.
Also reduce volume: send at 10-20 Hz or only on change, use FireAllClients except the sender, or skip relaying and let clients derive footsteps locally from character movement.
D16:
Problems:
- Message size limit 1 KB (1,024 chars encoded). A 3 KB table won't publish; you'd need to split it, which makes everything else worse.
- Receive limit per topic: about 40 + 80 x servers messages/min. 500 servers each publishing every 5 s = 6,000 msgs/min into one topic, and every one of the 500 subscribers receives each message (3M deliveries/min). That blows through the per-topic and experience-wide receive budgets (~400 + 200 x servers), so messages get throttled/dropped.
- Per-server publish limit (600 + 240 x players/min) and subscription limits (20 + 8 x players per server) also apply.
- Delivery is best effort: no guarantee, no ordering, ~1-2 s latency, and the sender receives its own messages. Servers that start late miss all history, and there is no "current state" to query.
- No TTL: a server that crashes leaves a stale entry until you add your own expiry.
Better: MemoryStoreService SortedMap (or HashMap) keyed by JobId, holding a compact summary (player count, map, region; not full player lists), with a ~60-90 s expiration refreshed every ~15-30 s. Browsers read pages of it with GetRangeAsync on demand. Mind MemoryStore memory quota (64 KB + 1.2 KB x users) and request units. Use MessagingService only for small, rare events.
D17:
Limits: HttpService allows 500 requests per minute per game server, for all HttpService calls combined (external and Open Cloud). 3 per join + 1 per kill on a busy server easily exceeds it, and then requests fail or stall (~30 s). Requests also yield and can fail at any time.
Correct setup:
- Enable "Allow HTTP Requests" for the experience (HttpEnabled).
- Batch analytics: queue events in memory and flush every 10-30 s as one POST, plus a final flush in game:BindToClose with a short timeout. Budget per server, not per player.
- Wrap calls in pcall. Retry only 408/425/429/5xx, with exponential backoff + jitter, honoring Retry-After. Don't retry other 4xx. Never let analytics block gameplay or saves (task.spawn).
- Secrets: never hard-code API keys. String literals ship with the place file (any collaborator, leaked copies, or require'd modules can read them). Store them in the experience's Secrets store (Creator Hub) and use HttpService:GetSecret("name"), which returns a Secret object you can pass to headers (e.g. with :AddPrefix) without exposing the plaintext. Rotate the leaked key now. Give it minimal scopes and restrict it to the experience.
- Consider Roblox's built-in AnalyticsService for in-game metrics so no HTTP is needed.
D18:
Client camera: Heartbeat (PostSimulation) fires after physics, out of step with rendering. The default camera script and the character's interpolated position update at a different point in the frame, so your CFrame write lands at an inconsistent time and the camera jitters. Use RunService:BindToRenderStep("FollowCam", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value + 1, fn), which runs just before rendering and after the default camera (pass the number, not the EnumItem). RenderStepped/PreRender also works for client visuals; unbind with UnbindFromRenderStep. Use dt to smooth (e.g. lerp with 1 - exp(-k*dt)).
Server projectile: RenderStepped/PreRender and BindToRenderStep exist only on the client (the server doesn't render), so they error on the server. Use RunService.Heartbeat (or PostSimulation) for step-after-physics logic, or PreSimulation to set physics state before the step, and use its deltaTime argument so motion is frame-rate independent. Simpler still: compute the trajectory analytically (or use raycasts per step) on the server and let clients render visuals. Summary: client visuals/camera -> render step; server game logic -> Heartbeat/PreSimulation/PostSimulation (or BindToSimulation under Server Authority).
D19:
Use the Input Action System (IAS) for a new cross-platform game in 2026. ContextActionService still works (BindAction isn't deprecated), but IAS is the forward path: declarative rebindable mappings that work on client and server, and it's required for Server Authority.
Structure (instances):
- InputContext: a group of actions you enable/disable as a unit (e.g. "Gameplay", "Menu"), with Priority and Sink for layering.
- InputAction (child of context): e.g. "Sprint" (Type Bool), "Interact" (Bool), or "Move" (Direction2D). Read with GetState() or the Pressed/Released/StateChanged events.
- InputBinding (child of action): a KeyCode (LeftShift, ButtonL3/ButtonX, E), modifiers, Scale. For touch, a UI button via binding (or a scriptable binding fired with InputBinding:Fire; InputAction:Fire is deprecated).
Give every action keyboard, gamepad and touch bindings.
Default player scripts: Roblox is migrating the PlayerModule control/camera scripts to IAS via Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem. Phase 1 (June 2026): opt-in. Phase 2 (early 2027, planned): on by default. Phase 3 (mid 2027, planned): the property is removed and IAS player scripts are the only option. Code that hooks PlayerModule:GetControls() or relies on old CAS input sinking will break. If you fork the player scripts, set StarterPlayer.CreateDefaultPlayerModule appropriately and keep them up to date.
D20:
Enable it on Workspace: AuthorityMode = Server (opt-in, released July 2026). Turning it on forces related settings: NextGenerationReplication, PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem, SignalBehavior = Deferred, StreamingEnabled and UseFixedSimulation.
What it does: the server is authoritative over physics and character simulation instead of trusting client-owned network ownership. Clients run the same simulation code locally to predict their own movement/actions immediately. When the server's result differs, the client rolls back and resimulates to the server state. This removes the classic client-owned exploits (teleport, fly, fling, speed hacks) at the engine level while keeping responsiveness.
Script changes:
- Put simulation/gameplay-step code in a ModuleScript that both server and client load, and register it with RunService:BindToSimulation(fn) (fixed timestep), not Heartbeat/RenderStepped.
- Read input through the Input Action System (InputActions), not UserInputService/CAS.
- Use time() (not tick/os.clock) and keep code deterministic. Predicted state goes in attributes (limits: ~64 attributes, names/strings 50 chars).
- In bound functions, don't Destroy, reparent or EquipTool. Use Player:GetCameraState() for aim. Guard VFX/sounds with RunService:IsResimulating() so they don't replay.
- SetNetworkOwner tricks aren't an equivalent and should be removed. Re-test with Deferred signals.
D21:
The API is RunService:BindToSimulation(callback), running with the fixed-step simulation (Workspace.UseFixedSimulation). Custom movement registered this way runs at a fixed simulation rate with a constant timestep, independent of render FPS, on both client and server. A 30 FPS and a 144 FPS player then integrate identically, and the server reproduces the client's results (prediction/resimulation under Server Authority).
Requirements:
- Enable fixed simulation (Workspace.UseFixedSimulation; it is forced on by AuthorityMode = Server, which this API is built around).
- Same code on both sides: put the step in a ModuleScript required by server and client, and bind it on both.
- Deterministic step: use only the provided fixed dt, time() rather than tick/os.clock, and input read through the Input Action System (InputAction states), not UserInputService events.
- Keep simulated state in attributes/physics so it can be rolled back. The callback may run several times per frame during resimulation, so make it side-effect free (no Destroy/reparent; guard effects with RunService:IsResimulating()).
Without it, the fallback is a hand-rolled fixed-step accumulator in PreSimulation: clamp dt, cap steps per frame, interpolate rendering.

Yes. Instance:QueryDescendants(selector) takes a CSS-like selector string and returns the matching descendants directly, so you don't need to walk GetDescendants and check tags/attributes in Lua:
```lua
local coins = workspace:QueryDescendants("BasePart.Coin[$Collected = false]")
for _, coin in coins do
    -- ...
end
```
Selector grammar: ClassName (matches IsA, so BasePart covers Part/MeshPart), .Tag (CollectionService tag), #Name, [Property = value], [$Attribute] / [$Attribute = value] for attributes, the combinators > (child) and >> (descendant), and :has(...) / :not(...).
For a set you keep watching, CollectionService:CreateCollection(query, root?) gives a live Collection (root defaults to Workspace) instead of re-querying every round. Alternatively CollectionService:GetTagged("Coin") plus an attribute check is far cheaper than GetDescendants. Note that a single :QueryDescendants call is a snapshot.
D24:
All four have built-ins now:
- lerp -> math.lerp(a, b, t) (a + (b - a) * t; doesn't clamp t).
- remap -> math.map(x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax) (linear, doesn't clamp; clamp afterwards with math.clamp if needed).
- NaN check -> math.isnan(x) (also math.isinf and math.isfinite). math.isfinite is the right guard for remote-supplied numbers, since NaN passes typeof and range checks. Never use x == math.nan.
- Bit packing -> buffer.writebits(b, bitOffset, bitCount, value) / buffer.readbits(b, bitOffset, bitCount): read/write arbitrary bit-width fields (bitCount 0-32) at a bit offset (0-based), so the 3-bit and 5-bit fields pack with no manual bit32 shifting/masking:
```lua
buffer.writebits(b, 0, 3, kind)  -- bits 0-2
buffer.writebits(b, 3, 5, level) -- bits 3-7
local kind = buffer.readbits(b, 0, 3)
```
Delete the hand-rolled versions; the built-ins are faster (native) and handle edge cases.
